answers.answer: The question is correct that the yarn PO does NOT solely control the realised pilling grade. My own kb3 PILLING_ACCEPTANCE_GATE (line 1256) states the ICI gate is run on 'a PPS swatch in the exact construction (fibre x twist x gauge), because pilling is jointly controlled and only the finished construction reveals the real grade.' So the honest decomposition is: the yarn PO CONTROLS the fibre-line inputs to pilling -- staple length (longer = less pill), twist (under-twist pills), ply (2-ply binds vs singles), fibre fineness / dpf (the anti-pill higher-dpf acrylic grade vs cheapest 1D), and the blend ratio -- these are my five spinning dials and they are genuinely won at the yarn PO [FACT: definitional, per glossary 'five spinning dials']. The yarn PO does NOT control gauge/stitch-density/knit-tightness (T3 machines / T8 construction) or the finishing route (T6), which co-determine the achieved grade. Therefore the precise, defensible claim is: the yarn PO sets the pilling FLOOR in the sense that it fixes the fibre/twist/ply/dpf/blend inputs that no downstream lever can fully recover -- a cheap short-staple low-twist 1D acrylic cannot be finished up to grade 3-4 -- but the FLOOR is a floor on INPUTS, not a guarantee of the realised post-wash grade, which stays [UNKNOWN]-UNTESTED until the PPS swatch in the exact construction (DECISION_MEMO G4). The specialist FILE currently phrases this as 'the anti-pill spec WON at the yarn PO (the pilling FLOOR)' (owns[]) and 'the post-wash pilling gate dominates any anti-pill adjective' (conflicts row 2), which is directionally correct but DOES over-attribute if read as 'the yarn PO alone determines the grade'. It should be tightened to 'the yarn PO sets the FIBRE-SIDE floor (staple/twist/ply/dpf/blend); the realised ICI grade is co-determined with construction (T3/T8) and finishing (T6) and stays [UNKNOWN] until the PPS swatch.' [FACT on the decomposition; the achieved grade [UNKNOWN]].

As written, 'WON at the yarn PO (the pilling FLOOR)' can be read as claiming the yarn PO determines the grade, which my own kb3 line 1256 contradicts. GAP: add the fibre-side-vs-construction split to owns[]/conflicts row 2 so the FLOOR is a floor on inputs, not an implied grade guarantee. This is a residual overclaim (a real finding), not something to fabricate a fix for.

answers.answer: My spec does NOT contain a written accept/reject rule for the case where a yarn-PO swatch grades 3 but a finishing route (cellulase bio-polish / singe) would lift the FINISHED post-wash grade to 3-4. This is a genuine gap at the yarn/finishing seam. What my spec DOES say resolves most of it in principle: kb3 PILLING_ACCEPTANCE_GATE (line 1256) requires the ICI gate to be graded 'on a PPS swatch in the exact construction (fibre x twist x gauge) ... only the finished construction reveals the real grade' AND '>= 1 home-wash cycle' -- i.e. the CONTRACTUAL gate is meant to be read on the finished, washed swatch, NOT on a bare off-loom yarn swatch. If the gate is graded on the finished-and-washed PPS swatch, then a bio-polish/singe that legitimately lifts the grade to 3-4 is ALREADY captured (the finished swatch grades 3-4 and passes) and there is no conflict. The unresolved case is narrower: grading a BARE yarn swatch at the yarn-PO stage BEFORE the construction+finishing is applied. For that, my spec has no explicit rule, so the honest answer is: the yarn-PO stage should grade an INDICATIVE bare-yarn/greige swatch as an early-warning screen, but the BINDING accept/reject is the finished-construction post-wash PPS grade (per kb3 1256), which INCLUDES the finishing route. Therefore the 'yarn floor dominates the finishing ceiling' claim (router) is best read as: finishing can buy only a FRACTION of a grade and cannot rescue a fibre/twist/ply/dpf choice that is structurally below floor (a cheap short-staple 1D acrylic will not reach 3-4 by bio-polish), but where finishing legitimately moves a borderline grade on cellulosic/hairy A1 the FINISHED swatch is the contract and no separate 'reject the yarn that finishing would save' rule is needed. The gap is that the spec never states this ordering explicitly, leaving the bare-yarn-vs-finished-swatch accept/reject ambiguous.

answers.gap_note: GAP: no explicit written accept/reject procedure distinguishing (a) the indicative bare-yarn/greige screen at the yarn-PO stage from (b) the binding finished-construction post-wash PPS grade that already includes the finishing route. Add that ordering so the yarn-floor-dominates-finishing rule is falsifiable at the boundary. No fabrication: the achieved grade stays [UNKNOWN] until the PPS swatch (G4).

answers.answer: The question exposes a real incompleteness in the veto. My spec vetoes OWNING/co-investing in a dyehouse absolutely (glossary 'no captive dyehouse', escalation_triggers 3), justified by the structural cluster closure-EXPOSURE mechanism: 'all three Ludhiana CETPs were found non-compliant, the CPCB levied crore-scale penalties and the NGT is reviewing the cluster, creating real closure exposure' [FACT enforcement, per glossary and kb2]. My sanctioned graduation is 'greige + job-work dye ... only for a proven hero colour' (capability 5, conflicts row 7). Honestly: job-work dyeing routes the brand's greige hero-colour yarn through a THIRD-PARTY dyer in the SAME closure-exposed cluster, so the OWNERSHIP veto neutralises balance-sheet/capital liability and CPCB/NGT penalty exposure, but it does NOT neutralise the SUPPLY-CONTINUITY risk: a job-work dyer under NGT review can be shut mid-lot, stranding the hero-colour greige. My spec does NOT write this distinction -- the veto stops at ownership and the continuity risk at the job-work step is unaddressed. This is described strictly as a structural regulatory mechanism (cluster-wide CETP non-compliance / NGT review), never an accusation against any named dyer. The correct, honest posture: 'never own a dyehouse' moves the CAPITAL/liability risk off the balance sheet but leaves the hero-colour supply exposed to the identical cluster shutdown; the job-work-dye graduation therefore needs a written continuity mitigation (dual-source the dye step, hold safety stock of the hero shade, or keep the hero colour on a bought-dyed fallback) that my spec currently lacks.

answers.answer: Correct -- my spec's sensitivity on the dye-lot MOQ floor is one-sided (benign) and does NOT model the floor materially ABOVE my band. The spec holds ~150-500 kg/colour as the binding constraint capping ~2-4 launch colours (capability 5, glossary 'dye-lot MOQ per colour', conflicts row 1), with a small-batch surcharge of +20-50% below the dye-house economic ~500-2,000 kg. The stress-test I carry only reassures that ~2-4 colours is robust to the floor rising a little (and improves if the true floor is well under ~150 kg). It does NOT model the material-upside case. Honestly, working the arithmetic in my own units: at ~300-400 g/sweater, ~150 kg is already ~375-500 sweaters of ONE colour, and ~500 kg is ~1,250-1,650 sweaters/colour. If a live dyer quote returned a floor of ~600-800 kg/colour (ABOVE my band), then at a micro-capsule's realistic total volume the line could NOT support 2 distinct launch colours per article without either the +20-50% small-batch surcharge or collapsing to essentially 1-2 shades TOTAL shared across all three articles [ESTIMATE: arithmetic on my own bands; the true floor [UNKNOWN] until a live dyer quote]. That downside is exactly the direction that SHRINKS the brand and is precisely what the 'sizes the brand' constraint should be stress-tested for, yet my spec does not model it. This does not change the dominant framing (dye-lot MOQ, not yarn price, sizes the brand) -- it strengthens it -- but the launch colour count I hand to line-planning is structurally OVER-optimistic if the real floor is higher than my band. The mitigations already in my spec (share dye lots across styles, launch on bought-dyed stock shades where the supplier carries the dye-lot, reserve one proven hero colour) are exactly the levers that soften a HIGH floor, but the spec never connects them to the high-floor case.

answers.answer: The R1 two-axis tie-break (post-wash pilling gate = HARD accept/reject VETO; dye-lot MOQ = SIZING cap; they act on different axes) does NOT fully resolve the three-way collision the question poses, and I concede the dye-METHOD axis is left partly unadjudicated. Walking the raised lot -- a proven hero colour available ONLY as a bought-dyed stock shade that grades ICI 3 post-wash, VS the same fibre available as greige (job-work-dyeable to the hero colour) that could reach 3-4 via an anti-pill finishing route: my spec's ordering gives a PARTIAL resolution. First, the pilling VETO binds absolutely (conflicts row 2, router pilling dominance): a bought-dyed shade that grades ICI 3 post-wash on the finished construction FAILS and is rejected outright -- the hero colour cannot ship at grade 3 regardless of MOQ or dye convenience. That is decisive and removes the bought-dyed-3 option. What my spec does NOT cleanly adjudicate is the surviving branch: the ONLY way to GET the hero colour at 3-4 is the greige + job-work-dye route, which my dye call DEFAULTS AGAINST (launch on bought-dyed; graduate to greige+job-work only for a proven hero worth the MOQ and shade-management, conflicts row 7). Here the pilling fix REQUIRES the greige route the dye default resists, so the two rules point opposite ways and my spec has no written rule that says 'when the only passing-grade path is greige+job-work, the pilling veto OVERRIDES the bought-dyed default'. The honest resolution -- consistent with my dominance ordering but not currently WRITTEN -- is: the pilling veto is the hard gate and dominates the dye-method PREFERENCE, so if the hero colour only clears the gate via greige+job-work, the brand graduates to greige+job-work for that colour (accepting the added dye-lot MOQ, shade-consistency and cluster continuity risk from R2Q7), because a shippable grade is non-negotiable while bought-dyed-vs-greige is a preference. But my decision_procedure step 7 and conflicts rows 1/2/7 do not chain these three axes explicitly, so the file only cleanly covers the two-way (veto-then-size) case, not this three-way (veto forces a dye-method the default resists) case.

answers.answer: This is a genuine cross-constraint tension my spec does not reconcile. The climate inversion (warm Turlock sells light/mid knits ~Sept-April, heavy wool only Nov-Feb; glossary 'climate inversion') underwrites A3 as a deliberately THIN Nov-Feb merino/lambswool capsule (glossary 'A1/A2/A3 line'). Working my own arithmetic: at ~300-400 g/sweater, ~150 kg is ~375-500 merino sweaters of ONE colour, and ~500 kg is ~1,250-1,650. A 'thin Nov-Feb capsule' in even a single merino colour must therefore be at least ~375-500 units of that shade just to clear the LOW end of the floor, or pay the +20-50% small-batch surcharge, or be bought-dyed-only [ESTIMATE: arithmetic on my own bands; true floor [UNKNOWN] until a live dyer quote]. So the two load-bearing constraints DO pull against each other for A3: the climate thesis wants A3 SMALL, while the dye-lot MOQ forces a per-colour MINIMUM that may exceed a genuinely thin capsule's volume -- making A3 either (a) forced LARGER than the climate thesis wants (over-committing merino inventory into a short Nov-Feb window -- a working-capital and markdown risk), (b) pushed to bought-dyed-stock-shade-only so the supplier carries the dye-lot (which my spec ALREADY defaults to, and which is the natural reconciliation), or (c) run at the small-batch surcharge. My spec does NOT explicitly reconcile 'A3 is deliberately thin' with 'A3 still needs ~150-500 kg/colour'. The available reconciliation IS latent in my own rules -- launch A3 on bought-dyed stock shades (supplier carries the dye-lot, so the thin capsule is not gated by MY dye-lot MOQ), keep A3 to ONE or very few shades, and share the merino base across styles -- but this is never stated as the resolution of the climate-vs-MOQ tension for the premium capsule. So I concede: the line architecture has an unreconciled tension at its halo article, softened (not eliminated) by the bought-dyed default, and the spec should state that A3's thinness is made MOQ-feasible specifically by keeping it bought-dyed-stock-shade and single/few-colour, not by a small standalone dye lot.
